items.title: Hourly workers are living with 7.86% inflation. No wonder they voted against the AI boom
items.summary:
On Nov. 3, in 40 of 41 local votes across 10 states, Americans chose to limit data centers. Many observers read that as voters choosing a recession over the biggest industrial buildout of their lifetimes .

I read it differently. Hourly workers are short on paycheck, and the warehouses near those data centers are short on hourly workers. The backlash and the buildout are one problem seen from two ends.

I see both ends because my company staffs those warehouses, which also means a tight labor market is good for our business. The figures below come from our shift and survey data unless I note otherwise.

Look at the paycheck 

Headline inflation was 3.7% in September . The Bureau of Labor Statistics itself says the CPI “ does not necessarily measure your own experience with price change .” For hourly workers, the gap is wide. In our survey of 3,083 hourly workers this summer , 69.4% said they earn under $30,000 a year across all their jobs, and only about half have a savings account.

So I rebuilt the number around how these workers spend. I call it FeelFlation. We took each category’s share of take-home pay and weighted it by how much that category’s cost rose in the 12 months through September (figures rounded):

Rent or mortgage: 28% of take-home pay, costs up 3% Interest on debt: 16%, up 21% Transportation: 15%, up 11% Discretionary spending: 13%, up 2.6% Food: 10.9%, up 3% Insurance premiums: 10%, up 12% Healthcare: 7%, up 2.6% 

The weighted total is 7.86%, more than double the headline. The interest increase is our estimate from Consumer Financial Protection Bureau…
items.t: Hourly workers are living with 7.86% inflation. No wonder they voted against the AI boom

items.title: ‘Dillon Brooks? On Kalshi? Hell nah’: LeBron James sues the sports betting app whose AI version of him said it
items.summary:
In an ad, LeBron James sits in an NBA locker room in a No. 23 jersey with “Bron” printed across the back, scrolling through bets on his phone. He stops on a photo of Phoenix Suns forward Dillon Brooks, one of his best-known on-court rivals. “Dillon Brooks? On Kalshi? Hell nah,” he says, in James’ voice.

Except it isn’t James. It’s an AI-generated version of him, made by a two-person startup to sell a sports betting app called Bron. And James, who has an exclusive endorsement deal with Kalshi-rival Polymarket, is now suing.

King James has been at the center of many notable brand deals—spanning massive contracts with Nike , Sprite , and of course, Polymarket . But the NBA’s oldest active player, and his company LBJ Trademarks LLC, is accusing the app’s creator PlayVision Inc. of exploiting his likeness in an AI-generated ad—and using an alleged affiliation with the star to promote itself.

The suit, filed on Nov. 17 in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York against the app’s parent company and its cofounders Anish Gupta and Marc Zoghby, 

alleges trademark infringement, false endorsement and false advertising. According to the complaint, the founders are PlayVision’s only employees, and it includes an argument that the company deliberately chose the name Bron and used an AI version of James in its marketing to capitalize on his global recognition.

“The word ‘Bron’ has no dictionary definition and no special meaning in the context of sports analytics, wagering, or artificial intelligence,” the filing read. “Rather, in the context of anything…
items.t: ‘Dillon Brooks? On Kalshi? Hell nah’: LeBron James sues the sports betting app whose AI version of him said it

items.title: Chris Christie says Jensen Huang shouldn’t come back to Nvidia. Hours later, the board agreed
items.summary:
On Tuesday morning, Jensen Huang said he’d return as Nvidia’s CEO if the board asked. By that afternoon, a possible 2028 Republican presidential candidate said he shouldn’t. A few hours later, Nvidia’s board said the same.

“No,” former New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie said when Fortune’s Diane Brady asked at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum whether Huang should return.

Christie lumped the former Nvidia CEO in with President Trump as an example of “people in positions of power without any character.” Speaking onstage with former Democratic Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum Tuesday, Christie, who is a Republican, railed against Huang’s behavior. 

“We have gone on a character holiday for 10 years,” he said. “We have said—because we have a leader in the White House and leaders throughout business like Jensen Huang who have said all that matters is the bottom line, and character doesn’t matter anymore.”

The White House did not immediately respond to Fortune ’s request for comment.

Huang steps down 

Huang stepped down as CEO of Nvidia last week after admitting he was unfaithful to his wife, amid reports of more than one extramarital relationship. The New York Times previously reported on his close relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence services suspected was a Chinese spy. China has denied the allegation.

Huang’s behavior, Christie implied Tuesday, was an example of the degradation of ethics that has taken over America during the past decade. President Trump was first elected president in 2016.

Trump, who has forged a close relationship…
items.t: Chris Christie says Jensen Huang shouldn’t come back to Nvidia. Hours later, the board agreed

items.title: The AI bubble is cracking. Wall Street is nervous
items.summary:
The AI gold rush as we knew it is over. The technology will keep advancing, but unlimited spending and unquestioned valuations is finished. The biggest threat to the AI boom sits in the financing that holds the ecosystem together. The trend line is heading precipitously down. Global AI funding was $239.1 billion in Q1 of 2026, $153.1 billion in Q2 and $103.3 billion in Q3. Is this the bottom? The company at the core of the AI industry may be key to finding that answer.

The great repricing has begun 

Nvidia has lost nearly $2 trillion in market value since its October 6 record, over 30% of what was the most valuable company on earth, gone in under six weeks. On Nov. 12, Jensen Huang resigned after 33 years. The CFO is interim CEO and Congress has called Huang to testify. The company at the center of the AI economy now carries succession risk and national security exposure at the same time. Recent earnings reports may have softened the sting, but questions still must be answered.

Having great technology does not justify every valuation. The people behind the tech must be able to responsibly steward a company and its mission.

The $570 billion question 

Bloomberg’s chart of circular AI financing puts Nvidia at the center of a global web that includes Microsoft , Google, Amazon , OpenAI, Anthropic, Oracle and CoreWeave. Billions move between them as equity stakes, chip purchases, cloud contracts and guarantees. But, how much of this demand is organic and how much is financed by the companies that benefit from it?

Chipmakers invest in AI companies, which buy their chips.…
items.t: The AI bubble is cracking. Wall Street is nervous

items.title: JD Vance says Americans don’t need to stock up. The Pentagon and U.S. allies are preparing for the worst
items.summary:
Vice President JD Vance has a message for Americans wondering whether a week of cascading outages signals worse to come: Skip the bunker.

“A lot of my friends have reached out asking if they should prepare to build a bunker or stock up on food and water,” Vance told Fox News host Laura Ingraham on Monday, in an interview covered by the New York Post . “My answer to that is no. We don’t see a crisis coming down. But you have to be prepared for everything.”

That advice puts Washington at odds with several close allies, which are telling their citizens the opposite. And it lands on a public that, after six days in which Microsoft, the nation’s air traffic system, major banks, Apple, and the National Security Agency all stumbled, has good reason to wonder whom to believe.

Six days, five failures 

The run began November 12 with a massive Exchange Online outage that rippled across Microsoft 365 services. The next afternoon, the FAA halted flights across U.S. airspace for nearly five hours after data flooded its legacy telecom network, and the agency says it has no indication of a cyberattack .

On November 16, customers of JPMorgan Chase, Wells Fargo, Capital One, and other banks couldn’t get to their money . Chase told Time the cause was “a software bug in on-premise hardware systems” and that “there is no evidence this is cyber-related.”

A day later, Apple said a faulty internal update knocked out iCloud and other customer services, and the NSA said its classified internal network suffered a “temporary degradation” during routine maintenance.

Officials insist the…
items.t: JD Vance says Americans don’t need to stock up. The Pentagon and U.S. allies are preparing for the worst

items.title: The CEO behind Grand Theft Auto VI doesn’t play video games, but analysts say he has put $1.5 billion behind the biggest game launch of the decade
items.summary:
After 15 years churning out hit titles like Grand Theft Auto, Red Dead Redemption , and NBA2k, this CEO knows what makes a hit—even if he doesn’t play video games himself. 

Strauss Zelnick, a Harvard Law School and Harvard Business School graduate, has been CEO of Take-Two Interactive Software since 2011. During that time, he has helped skyrocket the company’s stock price by more than 1,700% from about $12 per share when he took charge to about $221 per share as of Wednesday. He has also quintupled the company’s net revenue during his tenure, with 2025’s full-year number coming in at $5.6 billion compared with less than $1 billion before he took over.

He has been massively successful at the game publisher in the past and is preparing for what could be his biggest success yet with this week’s release of Grand Theft Auto VI. This is all despite the fact he doesn’t play the games he helps bring to life.

He may watch others play, but he doesn’t think it’s necessary that he be the one holding the controller, he told Business Insider earlier this year.

“I don’t think being consumer-in-chief really helps a CEO be effective in this business,” he said.

For the leader of a company selling a vice-laden game, Zelnick’s habits are tame. The Take-Two CEO doesn’t drink, smoke, and works out nearly every day, and sometimes twice a day, Business Insider reported. 

Now, Take-Two and Zelnick are preparing to release Grand Theft Auto VI, one of the most anticipated releases of the year, amid increasing competition and economic uncertainty.

Zelnick said pre-orders for the game were…
items.t: The CEO behind Grand Theft Auto VI doesn’t play video games, but analysts say he has put $1.5 billion behind the biggest game launch of the decade

items.title: Oklahoma’s governor sees universities as ‘stuck in their ways.’ His fix, a 3-year bachelor’s degree, is already spreading fast
items.summary:
Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt has a problem with the four-year degree, and he brought it to a room full of the people who hire its graduates.

“The academic community are kind of stuck in their ways. They don’t like to change,” Stitt said Monday at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit, on a panel with U.S. Steel CEO David Burritt. He said when he digs into the degree programs at the University of Oklahoma and Oklahoma State, “there’s a book this thick and then you’ve got like three people graduating from these different things.” 

He added: “I’m not saying that degree is not important, but you can’t be all things [to] all people.”

His fix is a 90-credit bachelor’s degree, 30 credits short of the standard 120, or roughly a year less of tuition. In-state tuition and fees at public four-year colleges averaged $11,950 in the 2024-25 school year, according to the College Board. Stitt said the idea is to keep the rigor of the requirements, trim some electives, and “get kids ready for the workforce quicker.”

RAND counted 119 reduced-credit bachelor’s programs publicly announced across the U.S. as of May 2026, up from five in 2024, most of them in “applied and workforce-facing fields.” Jason Lee, a senior policy researcher at RAND, has since told the Wall Street Journal the number of shortened bachelor’s programs announced this year are up to roughly 150.

From executive order to diploma 

Stitt signed an executive order in February ordering a 90-day study of 90-credit “accelerated” degrees, and the Legislature followed with HB 3315, which required the State Regents to study…
items.t: Oklahoma’s governor sees universities as ‘stuck in their ways.’ His fix, a 3-year bachelor’s degree, is already spreading fast

items.title: Home Depot’s incoming CEO says homeowners are ‘feeling pressure.’ A quarter can’t cover a $5,000 repair
items.summary:
Richard McPhail, a 21-year Home Depot veteran who was named the retailer’s next CEO on Tuesday, has been watching financial pressure build among American homeowners. On the company’s third-quarter earnings call the same day, he acknowledged that “a rising interest rate environment puts pressure on our customer and our business.”

McPhail, Home Depot’s CFO since 2019, takes over as CEO on Nov. 23. Ted Decker, who recently returned from a medical leave, will step down as CEO and remain chair of the board.

That’s a problem for a retailer that booked $164.7 billion in revenue last fiscal year, the bulk of it from people fixing up homes they already own. Homeowners are “one of the most resilient customer cohorts in the economy,” McPhail told Yahoo Finance in a February interview. “But they’re feeling pressure like everyone else.”

“If you look at housing turnover, that’s actually been frozen for three years,” he said, adding that turnover has sat at historical lows three years running. He also pointed to customers’ “concerns around housing affordability, general affordability” and “broader concerns over uncertainty and job loss.”

Wealthy on paper, stretched in practice 

Owning a home has long been considered a path to financial security in America. But even homeowners with considerable housing wealth feel squeezed by the rising cost of living, and some struggle to afford the upkeep of their biggest asset.

Nearly two-thirds of homeowners (63%) say owning a home causes them at least moderate financial stress, up from 55% in June 2025, according to an October survey of 1,000…
items.t: Home Depot’s incoming CEO says homeowners are ‘feeling pressure.’ A quarter can’t cover a $5,000 repair

items.title: The reboot of poor Jensen Huang almost worked. But who can explain away 30 leather jackets? | Emma Brockes
items.summary:
He seemed like the thinking person’s tech titan. But then came the affairs, the share collapse – and of course, the sorry items in his wardrobe

A few years ago, I attended a small dinner at a friend’s house in the US at which a tech billionaire was the guest of honour. He wasn’t one of the most famous tech billionaires – I’d never heard of him, although I used his communications platform every day. Nonetheless, it was exciting to get up close to someone that staggeringly rich to see if he was different from the rest of us.

And he was different, sort of. Leaning back in his chair, he seemed to suggest, in a bored kind of way, that in the event of a US standoff with Russia, Putin nuking London would be the sort of collateral damage Washington could tolerate. A bit of an odd thing to say to a stranger. He didn’t observe the usual rules of conversation but rather, like a Roman emperor waiting to be entertained, remained belligerently aloof.

Emma Brockes is a Guardian columnist

Continue reading...
items.t: The reboot of poor Jensen Huang almost worked. But who can explain away 30 leather jackets? | Emma Brockes

items.title: We made GTA 6, the world’s biggest video game – we should have working conditions to match | Nestor Uriarte
items.summary:
After the release of Grand Theft Auto VI this week, Rockstar employees like me can make history again. We need union recognition to safeguard our jobs

When I first got the call offering me a job at Rockstar, I was thrilled. I thought back to being a child and sneaking into my brother’s room to grab the PlayStation Portable so I could secretly play Grand Theft Auto: Vice City Stories. The same kid who fell in love with Rockstar’s games back then now gets to spend every day helping to create those worlds as an animation programmer at the studio in Edinburgh. This week, we will celebrate the culmination of more than a decade of effort: the release of the most anticipated game of all time, Grand Theft Auto VI.

But our team has the opportunity to make history a second time this month. Right now, the ballot is open for Rockstar employees to decide whether we want the union we have built with our colleagues to get recognition. As someone who cares deeply about our team, cares about what we do, and wants us to be able to keep delivering world-class games into the future, I’m voting yes.

items.title: The Guardian view on the Milburn report: a manifesto for youth participation | Editorial
items.summary:
This is not a rerun of failed welfare cuts, but young people who rely on benefits cannot be expected to take promised opportunities on trust

The gap between the state’s investment in young people compared with older generations has more than doubled in two decades. At the same time, the number of 16- to 24-year-olds who are neither in education, employment or training (Neet) has climbed to 1 million. In Europe, only Romania has a higher Neet rate.

Alan Milburn’s message is that this amounts to a “moral crisis” which the British state must urgently address. Asked to write a review about young people and work, he has produced a “manifesto” for placing the broken social contract between generations at the heart of government. On Tuesday, his proposals for far-reaching changes to welfare, health, education and employment were on their way to becoming government policy as he was chosen to lead a new Youth Opportunities Unit.

items.title: The Guardian view on climate and debt: a vicious cycle the world must break at Cop31 | Editorial
items.summary:
Poor countries are paying creditors instead of preparing for climate disasters. The international financial system must stop deepening their vulnerability

The catastrophe that struck Nepal’s Himalayas in August began with a collapsing glacier. An avalanche of ice and rock unleashed deadly floods, sweeping away villages, bridges and roads, and leaving thousands dead or missing. It illustrated the dangers posed by global heating to the Himalayas’ increasingly unstable glaciers. Nepal lost a tenth of its electricity generation. Reconstruction will cost about $5bn. Yet the Loss and Damage Fund, hailed as a historic breakthrough at the 2022 UN climate summit, has earmarked just $20m for Nepal – less than 5% of the $482m that Kathmandu must pay its external public creditors this year.

items.title: Will the Milburn review come good or go south? Either way, we’ll always have Eurovision
items.summary:
The announcement of state plans to engage with young people told us nothing we hadn’t already heard, but it still felt momentous

It’s one of the country’s worst kept secrets. There can’t be anyone left who hasn’t heard of Alan Milburn’s Neets review, let alone read most of it too. It feels as if it’s become part of the fabric of our society for the past six months. There will be a Neets-shaped hole in our lives when it’s over.

Not a day has gone by without some part of it being leaked to the media. Seldom has a pitch been so icomprehensively rolled. Milburn has been out and about giving interviews to everyone – regardless of whether they wanted one or not. I rather suspect the reason Royal Mail lied about calling to collect my parcel return yesterday was because the driver found himself cornered by Milburn for a couple of hours and was unable to complete his round. Either that, or Royal Mail has a fleet of vans crisscrossing the country whose sole purpose is to make sure they never deliver anything. Ghost vans.

items.title: ‘What if the input isn’t the news? What if the input is you?’ Bill Gross gave away 1.2 million AI business ideas for free—the Fortune 500 is next
items.summary:
A month ago, Idealab founder Bill Gross gave away 1.2 million AI-generated business ideas for free. Now he wants Fortune 500 companies to pay $250,000 a year to run the same system on their own patents.

“What if the input isn’t the news? What if the input is you?” Gross told executives at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit on Monday, in a session sponsored by Idealab.ai. He meant their patents, trade secrets and “all the things that you’ve shelved inside of your company.” Idealab.ai plans to license the full system to companies at $250,000 a year, he said, and is offering five companies a one-year pilot for $25,000.

The pitch is aimed at a real problem: big companies hold a lot of patents that never become products. Large firms’ patents are tied to new product launches “far less so” than smaller firms’, according to research from Kellogg’s Sara Moreira and economists at Yale and the Atlanta Fed, which matched about 1.4 million products to patents. Moreira’s explanation complicates Gross’s pitch, though: big companies often use patents as a “defensive tool” to block competitors rather than to launch anything. Some of that shelved R&D is on the shelf on purpose.

The Caltech test 

Gross launched Idealab.ai in October after feeding an AI system news stories going back to 2000, every patent since 1980, product recalls, and complaints on Reddit and X, along with his own 31 methods for coming up with business ideas. He said it came back with 1.2 million ideas after about a month and roughly $1 million in AI costs, and that 131,000 people in 202 countries have…

items.title: Top Chamber of Commerce official says the midterms weren’t just about prices: They were about 20 years of 2% growth
items.summary:
Less than two weeks after voters handed Democrats both chambers of Congress in an election defined by frustration over the cost of living and perceived corruption , the U.S. Chamber of Commerce’s top policy official warned a room of executives that Washington might already be misreading the message.

Neil Bradley, the Chamber’s executive vice president, chief policy officer and head of strategic advocacy, said Monday at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit that the affordability anger is real. He also argued it sits on top of something voters have been signaling for two decades that “no one has been paying attention to”: 20 years of roughly 2% real GDP growth, after 60 years of more than 3%.

That gap is the difference between a kid who grows up richer than their parents and one who doesn’t. Harvard economist Raj Chetty and his co-authors found in a 2017 paper that the share of Americans earning more than their parents fell from about 90% for children born in 1940 to 50% for children born in the 1980s.

“The concept of the American dream isn’t 3% growth, but it’s highly correlated to it,” Bradley said.

The easy button 

Bradley’s real target was what Congress does next. “There’s a real temptation to hit the easy button,” he said, like capping credit card interest rates, price controls on pharmaceuticals, or limits on stock buybacks and dividends. These are “proposals that both ends of the political horseshoes are coming together on” and they might ease voters’ angst “for a brief period of time,” he said, “but they won’t solve our long-term challenges.”
